name: Unix time converter
seoTitle: Unix time converter Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Unix time converter: work out unix time from the CET. A free conversion calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The unix time converter takes the numbers you enter and reports unix time immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. That makes it useful for a recipe, a shopping list, a travel plan or a form that asks for a unit you do not use. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Unix time converter calculator work?
sections.html:
The Unix time converter takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports unix time in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you give the CET.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html: • A date and a time of day. Use the picker; the answer is recalculated the moment the date changes, and the count is done date-to-date rather than by subtracting timestamps.

sections.title: The formula behind the Unix time converter calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Unix time=UTC ÷ GMT
UTC/GMT=CET − 3600000
Eet/uz 1=UTC ÷ GMT + 7200000
MSK/EAT=UTC ÷ GMT + 10800000
SMT/AZT/GET/AMT/MUT=UTC ÷ GMT + 14400000
PKT/YEKT/MVT=UTC ÷ GMT + 18000000

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Time, opening in seconds

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Unix time converter earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Reading a recipe written in units you do not use
  • Filling in a form that asks for imperial or metric values
  • Checking a product listing against the measurements you work with
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the CET — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.

faq.q: What does the Unix time converter calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns unix time, derived from the CET. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Unix time converter calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the CET, which is a single field. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter unix time in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Unix time opens in seconds and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Unix time = -999.9972 sec. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Unix time converter calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
